intro.text: A walled complex in T'Telir, the capital of Hallandren, that serves as both home and parliament for the Returned. The gods effectively rule the nation from here, yet they are confined within its walls.

description.text: When Hallandren need a quality such as courage or boldness, they make offerings to a chosen god, usually paintings or other artwork. Priests write down what each god says and thinks of the pieces, and they arrange the Breath their gods need to go on living and blessing people.

Because the Returned may not leave, priests argue in the arena to keep them informed of what ordinary people want. A standing Court Assembly, made up mostly of priests and priestesses, meets daily for smaller rulings, and gods often attend to watch. About two dozen gods live here, the God King among them.

The grounds are essentially one huge lawn with no permanent gardens; when a god asks, gardeners bring in plants and lay out temporary flower beds. In the warm climate the gods' palaces are divided by little more than cloth, and their guards go unarmed, there only to turn away anyone without business inside. Shelters near the gates let visitors stay the night.

The God King's palace is built of black stone. Since he stands for every colour, each inner room he uses is filled with silks and tiles of a single hue, while the servants' outer area stays black. Few rooms have a fixed purpose: servants carry furniture in as it is needed, so almost everything, bathtubs included, is portable.

items.text: Once Peacegiver had ended the war, he handed his Breath to a priest in T'Telir, who became the first God King. With the royal family driven out, the Cult of the Returned took charge and formed the Court of Gods.

Every God King who followed bore the name Susebron. The third gave his life and Breath to save the children of a village that had been raided; the fourth died curing a plague of distrentia. The fifth then took the throne.
The Court agreed a treaty with Idris under which King Dedelin would send a daughter to marry the God King. An heir with royal blood would strengthen the Court's claim to rule Hallandren.

For three years, no god had given up their divine Breath to heal anyone. A rebel named Vahr challenged it, backed by several slumlords and by Idris through its agent Lemex. He was captured and kept alive in the Court's dungeons, tortured for his Breath, until he was killed there.
Rather than his eldest daughter, Vivenna, Dedelin sent the youngest, Siri. The choice unsettled the Court and fed talk of war.

Had Idris sent no one, open war would have followed. Opponents of war called the Idrian lands cold and not worth having; its supporters wanted to secure trade routes whose loss would wreck T'Telir's economy.
Siri's arrival began the Wedding Jubilation, a week of celebration at the Court, which had gone thirty years without a queen.
